### Problem: The Number of Weak Characters in the Game {#sec-salgo-p5-b}

::: {.p-statement}

Each character has `properties[i] = [attack, defense]` ($2 \le n \le 10^5$, $1 \le \mathit{attack}, \mathit{defense} \le 10^5$). A character $i$ is **weak** if some other character $j$ has *both* $\mathit{attack}_j > \mathit{attack}_i$ **and** $\mathit{defense}_j > \mathit{defense}_i$. Return the number of weak characters.

Source: [LC 1996 · The Number of Weak Characters in the Game](https://leetcode.com/problems/the-number-of-weak-characters-in-the-game/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}

Example — `[[5,5],[6,3],[3,6]]` → `0`; `[[1,5],[10,4],[4,3]]` → `1` (only $[4,3]$, beaten by $[10,4]$).
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
"$j$ dominates $i$ on both axes" is 2-D dominance. Brute force is every pair. The sorting move collapses it to a running maximum: sort by attack ascending and, while sweeping, the question "is there a *strictly larger attack* with larger defense?" becomes "does the maximum defense among strictly-larger-attack characters exceed mine?" — answerable in one right-to-left pass with a single scalar. The entire difficulty lives in **how ties in attack are ordered**, because a same-attack peer must not be allowed to "dominate."
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **All-pairs test.** For each $i$, scan for a $j$ beating it on both axes. $O(n^2)$ — the oracle, too slow at $10^5$.
2. **Sort + running-max sweep.** Sort by `(attack ascending, defense descending)`. Sweep right-to-left tracking the maximum defense seen so far. Because equal-attack rows are ordered defense-*descending*, when you are at a row, everything to its right has *strictly greater attack* (never an equal-attack peer), so a right-side defense greater than yours is a genuine dominator. Count it and move on. $O(n \log n)$.

**Invariant.** After sorting `(attack ↑, defense ↓)`, at any position the set of rows to the right is exactly the rows with strictly greater attack **or** equal attack and $\le$ defense; the defense-descending tie-break removes the equal-attack rows from ever being counted as dominators, so `max_defense_right > my_defense` iff a true dominator exists.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### All-pairs test

::: {.form-next}
For each character, look for any other that beats it on both attack and defense. $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ extra. The definition, and the checker for the sweep.

**Worked example.** $[[1,5],[10,4],[4,3]]$: $[4,3]$ is beaten by $[10,4]$ ($10>4$ and $4>3$); $[1,5]$ is beaten by nobody ($[10,4]$ has lower defense); $[10,4]$ highest attack → count 1.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("weak", "brute")
    assert str(final) == "1"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def wc1996_brute(props):
    n = len(props)
    return sum(1 for i in range(n)
               if any(i != j and props[j][0] > props[i][0] and props[j][1] > props[i][1]
                      for j in range(n)))
```

##### C++

```cpp
// all-pairs dominance test, O(n^2) oracle
int wc1996Brute(const vector<vector<int>>& p) {
    int n = (int)p.size(), weak = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j)
            if (i != j && p[j][0] > p[i][0] && p[j][1] > p[i][1]) { ++weak; break; }
    return weak;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `break` stops at the first dominator — we only need existence, not a count of dominators. The $O(n^2)$ is exactly the $n = 10^5$ wall, and note the attack/defense values are $\le 10^5$ so no overflow worries here.

#### Sort + running-max sweep

::: {.form-next}
Sort by attack ascending, and for equal attack by defense **descending**. Sweep right-to-left holding `best` = the maximum defense seen so far (which all belong to strictly-greater-attack characters, thanks to the tie-break). If my defense `< best` I am weak; then `best = max(best, my defense)`. $O(n \log n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra beyond the sort.

**Worked example.** $[[1,5],[10,4],[4,3]]$ sorted `(attack↑,defense↓)` = $[[1,5],[4,3],[10,4]]$. Right-to-left: $[10,4]$ sets `best=4`; $[4,3]$: $3<4$ → weak, `best=4`; $[1,5]$: $5\not<4$ → not weak. Total 1.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("weak", "sort")
    assert str(final) == "1"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-salgo-1996-sort
def wc1996_sort(props):
    order = sorted(props, key=lambda q: (q[0], -q[1]))   # attack asc, defense DESC
    weak = 0
    best = 0                                             # max defense among strictly-greater attack
    for _, d in reversed(order):
        if d < best:
            weak += 1
        best = max(best, d)
    return weak

for _ in range(200):
    ps = [[random.randint(1, 30), random.randint(1, 30)] for _ in range(random.randint(2, 25))]
    assert wc1996_sort(ps) == wc1996_brute(ps)
assert wc1996_sort([[5, 5], [6, 3], [3, 6]]) == 0
assert wc1996_sort([[2, 2], [3, 3]]) == 1
assert wc1996_sort([[1, 5], [10, 4], [4, 3]]) == 1
print("wc1996_sort OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
// sort (attack asc, defense desc), then right-to-left running max of defense
int wc1996Sort(vector<vector<int>> p) {
    sort(p.begin(), p.end(), [](const vector<int>& a, const vector<int>& b) {
        if (a[0] != b[0]) return a[0] < b[0];
        return a[1] > b[1];                       // defense DESC on equal attack: the crux
    });
    int weak = 0, best = 0;
    for (int i = (int)p.size() - 1; i >= 0; --i) {
        if (p[i][1] < best) ++weak;
        best = max(best, p[i][1]);
    }
    return weak;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The `defense DESC` tie-break is the entire subtlety: with equal-attack rows sorted by decreasing defense, a row's *right* neighbours never include an equal-attack character with larger defense — so `best` only ever aggregates strictly-greater-attack defenses, exactly the dominators. Reverse the tie-break to ascending and same-attack characters would falsely dominate each other; the stress test over random pairs (where ties are common) catches that instantly. `best` starts at 0 since all defenses are $\ge 1$.
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**All-pairs** is $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ space. **Sort + sweep** is $O(n \log n)$ time, $O(1)$ auxiliary. The sort-to-enable-a-scan is the same family as @sec-salgo-p5-a's key design — a well-chosen order turns a search into a running maximum.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- Many equal attacks: the defense-descending tie-break is what keeps them from dominating one another (need *strictly* greater on both axes).
- All identical characters → 0 weak.
- A strictly increasing ladder $[[1,1],[2,2],\dots]$ → every but the last is weak.
:::

::: {.practice}
- [LC 354 · Russian Doll Envelopes](https://leetcode.com/problems/russian-doll-envelopes/){difficulty="Hard"} — sort width ascending and height *descending*, then a longest increasing subsequence on heights: the same tie-break, for the same reason.
- [LC 406 · Queue Reconstruction by Height](https://leetcode.com/problems/queue-reconstruction-by-height/){difficulty="Medium"} — sort height descending, ties by $k$ ascending, then insert by index; the tie order decides whether the greedy works.
:::
